messages.subject: Piecewise Regression with multiple predictors
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm working on a project where I'm interested in estimating community index thresholds (e.g., functional diversity) for multiple predictors. With that in mind, I'm implementing a sort of piecewise regression model in JAGS. Ideally, I'd like to be able to include other predictors in the model but they would only be represented as standard betas in the model (i.e., not estimating threshold parameters for them). If I only include the predictor for which I wish to estimate the threshold response (in the code below "TWY"), the model runs fine in JAGS. However, if I include the other predictors as standard betas in the model, the following error is produced " Dimension mismatch, taking subset of stream1". I know this has to do with the inclusion of the other predictors, I just cannot seem to identify the  root cause of the error. Also, one more question along that same line: would it be possible to include multiple predictors for which I wish to estimate multiple threshold responses in the same model? This seems to be possible in R, but I cannot find any BUGS code to fit a similar model in JAGS.

As always, any help provided is more than appreciated!

Thanks,

Josh

Code below, data attached

#Upload Data
data<-read.csv("LS_Summer_dat.csv", header = T)

y<- (data[,7])/100
n<-nrow(data)
site<- nrow(data)

#Predictors
Stream1<- data[8]
Stream2<- data[9]
Land1<- data[10]
Land2<- data[11]
TWY<- standardize(data[,12])

#data for covariate model
jags.data<-list(y=y,n.sites=n,M=site, Stream1=Stream1, Stream2=Stream2,
                Land1=Land1, Land2=Land2, TWY=TWY)

########################
########################
require(jagsUI)
sink("model1.txt")
cat("
 model{
 #priors

 phi~ dgamma(0.1,0.1)
 beta ~ dunif(-3,3)
 beta1 ~ dunif(-3,3)
 beta2 ~ dunif(-3,3)
 beta3 ~ dunif(-3,3)
 beta4 ~ dunif(-2,2)
 x.change ~ dunif(-2,2)

 #Random Intercepts
 mu_int~dnorm(0, 0.001) # Mean hyperparameter for random intercepts
 sd_int~dunif(0, 1) # SD hyperparameter for random intercepts
 tau_int <- 1/(sd_int*sd_int)

 for (i in 1:M) {
    alpha0[i]~ dnorm(mu_int, tau_int)
 }

 #likelihood
 for(i in 1:n.sites) {
  y[i] ~ dbeta(a[i], b[i])
  a[i] <- mu[i] * phi
  b[i]  <- (1-mu[i]) * phi
  logit(mu[i])<-alpha0[i] + beta*Stream1[i] + beta1*Stream2[i]
   + beta2*Land1[i] + beta3*Land2[i] +
  beta4*(TWY[i]-x.change)*step(TWY[i] - x.change)
 }
 }
  ",fill=TRUE)
sink()

##Parameters to Estimate
params<-c("mu_int","beta", "beta1","beta2", "beta3", "beta4","x.change")

model1 <- jagsUI(data=jags.data, parameters.to.save=params,
                 model.file="model1.txt",n.thin =10,n.chains = 3,
                 n.burnin = 10000, n.iter =500000,parallel=TRUE)

messages.subject: Random intercepts/slopes with few group members
messages.subject_clean: Random intercepts/slopes with few group members
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a few questions around using random slopes and intercepts in hierarchical models. I'm fitting a multistate CJS model with data collected from one species at three independent sites. I naturally want to fit a single model to the data, so I have stacked the three capture histories in a 3D array. I want to use a model with random intercepts and slopes on the survival, transition, and capture probabilities. My sites don't have the same number of individuals, with the sites having 430, 130, and 75 individuals.

I have fit a model with random intercepts and slopes like AHM2 3.3, but I'm not sure if this is valid with just three sites. When comparing the site-level estimates of survival, they are very similar to a fixed effects model, but the model doesn't really converge on the mean and standard deviation of the group means. I can imagine it'd be hard for the model to converge on a mean and variance when for each parameter there's only 3 values drawn from this distribution.

My main question is whether there is any cost incurred when fitting a random slopes and intercepts model with few group members? If not, is there still the benefit of more data informing the estimates because the sites with fewer observations are 'borrowing' strength from the sites with more observations?

If there's any literature on this topic, I'd love to read it. Most of the papers I've read with hyperpriors on community or metapopulation intercepts and slopes have quite a bit more than 3 members.

Kind regards,
Matt

messages.subject: Postdoctoral researcher position: Quantitative disease ecology
messages.subject_clean: Postdoctoral researcher position: Quantitative disease ecology
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

My collaborators and I are looking to recruit a postdoctoral researcher to work with us on a project related to management, disease, and advanced quantitative methods (details below). We would greatly appreciate it if you could circulate the ad below to anyone you think would be interested.

Thank you!

Grace

Postdoctoral researcher position:

Improving management and surveillance decisions related to white nose syndrome by accounting for imperfect detection and misclassification error

Massachusetts Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit (MA Coop Unit)

University of Massachusetts, Department of Environmental Conservation, Amherst, MA

Review of applications will begin 23 June 2021

Position start date Fall 2021

Position description Management decisions for emerging infectious diseases, endangered species, and invasive species depend on the true state of the system and must be made quickly to maximize opportunities for control. However, molecular detection methods, like any diagnostic test used in the detection of pathogens, may occasionally yield false negatives (i.e., when a sample appears negative but is truly positive) as well as ‘ambiguous,’ ‘uncertain,’ or ‘equivocal’ results (i.e., an inability to confidently classify a sample as negative or positive). Therefore, we are seeking to recruit a postdoctoral researcher that will develop quantitative tools to improve pathogen surveillance in the white nose syndrome (WNS) system. Specifically, we are looking for a postdoc to extend a novel statistical model that accounts for both imperfect and ambiguous pathogen detections and to apply this model to already collected WNS field data for parameter estimation. This is a one-year postdoctoral position with the possible extension to a second-year dependent on performance and funding.

This work is a collaboration among the USGS Amphibian Research Monitoring Initiative, USGS National Wildlife Health Center, the University of Vermont, and the Massachusetts Cooperative Research Unit. The postdoctoral researcher will explore optimal sampling designs for determining pathogen absence or eradication and will use simulations to explore the model’s accuracy, precision, bias, and coverage. This model will use both negative and uncertain detections to make inference about a site’s disease state, and the postdoc will extend this model to include temporally and spatially varying covariates that can improve estimation of model parameters. The model will be incorporated into a surveillance model to improve inference on the distribution of WNS and its causative agent, Pseudogymnoascus destructans (Pd). PIs on this project work in several other disease systems, and while this project is focused on the WNS system, we will help to ensure that this model can be used to improve the detection and management of emerging pathogens and invasive species more broadly.

We highly encourage people from historically underrepresented groups to apply. The postdoc will work closely with collaborators from the USGS and Refuge managers. Please note that the successful candidate will likely work remotely until covid occupancy limits are lifted.

The University of Massachusetts, Amherst (which ranks among the top public universities nationally) and the USGS Eastern Ecological Science Center at the SO Conte Anadromous Fish Research Lab are located in Western Massachusetts. The area offers a rich cultural environment in a rural setting close to major urban centers, with many great outdoor recreational opportunities.

Salary/Benefits The postdoctoral researcher will be provided:

1.     Annual salary of $55,000 plus benefits

2.     Travel funds to attend a national conference

3.     A supportive network of professionals that encourage work-life balance, promote mental health well-being, and focus on helping you achieve your career goals

4.     Professional development relevant to a career with the USGS but transferable to other agencies

5.     Mentoring, encouragement, and autonomy to ensure that they see and understand how their perspectives are vital to achieving the mission of the USGS

Duties The postdoctoral researcher will be expected to:

(1) Develop a statistical model that accounts for imperfect detection and misclassification error, while including biological realism (e.g., detection probability as a function of pathogen load)

(2) Explore the properties of the statistical model using simulations and Bayes Theorem (i.e., explore model accuracy, precision, bias, and coverage with variable sampling designs and parameter values)

(3) Apply the statistical model to available surveillance data of WNS across the US, which will provide an estimate of the probability of pathogen occupancy given the number of negative and uncertain samples at each location (i.e., risk assessment)

(4) Provide decision support for sites at risk of WNS, where the true state of the system determines the optimal decision

Eligibility

-   PhD in ecology, epidemiology, biology, math, statistics, wildlife, or other related field

Application To apply, please submit your application as a single PDF with the document name “YOUR LAST NAME-WNS postdoc app- 2021.pdf” in an email with the subject “WNS postdoc application” to Drs. Graziella DiRenzo at gdir...@umass.edu and Evan Grant at ehg...@usgs.gov. Please include in your application the following materials:

(1) a 300–600 word cover letter describing:

- your research interests and background

- why you are interested in this position

- your experience in disease ecology, Bayesian methods, statistical modeling, and simulations

- your career goals;

(2) a curriculum vitae or resume;

(3) the contact information (name, position, relationship to applicant, email, and phone number) for three references;

Please send questions to any of the project investigators listed below.

Project investigators

Dr. Graziella DiRenzo (gdir...@umass.edu), U.S. Geological Survey, MA Coop Unit

Dr. Evan H. C. Grant (ehg...@usgs.gov), U.S. Geological Survey, Eastern Ecological Science Center

Dr. Brittany A. Mosher, University of Vermont, Burlington

Dr. Robin Russell, U.S. Geological Survey, National Wildlife Health Center

Dr. Dan Walsh, U.S. Geological Survey, National Wildlife Health Center

Nondiscriminatory AA/EEO statement The University of Massachusetts provides equal employment opportunities to all employees and applicants for employment without regard to race, color, religion, gender, gender identity or expression, age, sexual orientation, national origin, ancestry, disability, military status, genetic information, pregnancy or a pregnancy-related condition, or membership in any other legally protected class. The University of Massachusetts complies with all applicable federal, state and local laws governing nondiscrimination in employment in every location in which the university operates.

--
Graziella Vittoria DiRenzo, PhD
She/her/ella
Assistant Unit Leader of Wildlife
United States Geological Survey
Massachusetts Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit

messages.subject_clean: Syntax error JAGSUI: Error parsing model file
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I’d like some advice on occupancy models.

I have collected detection/non-detection data (“1” and “0”) using 41 camera traps somewhere in a forest in Costa Rica.

My data focuses on a few species: jaguar, puma, peccary, agouti and paca. I also have a few variables that could influence detection (e.g. whether a camera was placed on a road or trail, nr. of days the camera was active, etc.) or occupancy (NDVI, distance to protected area, etc.).

My total dataset is only 6 months of sampling and is divided into a “wet” season (10 consecutive sampling occasions) and “dry” season (11 consecutive sampling occasions). The aim of my research is to see which variables influence occupancy of the different species, but also to see if this changes between the seasons.

So far, I have done several “single-species, single-season” models (using “unmarked” in R) but I would like to move on to more complicated approaches, such as community-level models. As a first step, I’m trying to adapt the model used by Salom-Pérez et al. (2021) in their paper about the MBC, which is a JagsUI approach. However, I get an error (Error in checkForRemoteErrors(val) : 3 nodes produced errors; first error: Error parsing model file: syntax error on line 105 near "") and my knowledge of occupancy modelling is not good enough to understand exactly what I’m doing (wrong) or how to fix this problem.

Is there someone in this group who wants to work with me, exchange ideas, or help me on my way? I have attached the model code in a text file. The error appears on the line that says: #Establishing the Hyperparameter for the intercept on detection(p). This is already in the beginning of the model.

Any suggestions or approach ideas are very welcome, thanks in advance!

Best,

Fleur Damen

messages.subject: Speeding up multistate models for joint live recapture and dead recovery data
messages.subject_clean: Speeding up multistate models for joint live recapture and dead recovery data
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I am currently reviewing a paper where they use IPM containing a multistate model for joint live recapture and dead recovery data, which calculates also permanent emigration. It is similar to models in Kery & Schaub 2012 (BPA), chapter 9.5., but there are more states (juv alive in, juv alive outside, ad alive in, ad alive outside, dead, not seen). This part of the model is very slow since it loops over individuals, making the models run ~ 2 weeks without convergence.

I had some ideas how to speed up the models using generalized m-arrays (would be 3-dimensional m-arrays). I am trying to figure out if this was already used/published somewhere? Do you know of anyone who successfuly transformed their multistate models into m-array formulation?

I've seen older messages in this group on the solution with Nimble (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10651-016-0353-z), but I am now interested in whether someone already implemented the m-array solution.

Thank you very much!

Tomas

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I noticed some studies use ring recoveries of birds killed by hunting in dead recovery models - i.e. they use it in these models as "observed death". That seems very incorrect to me, since it's a sample of birds whose life has been cut short, so it will bias (underestimate) the survival probabilities. I think much more correct would be to use the hunting data in the models as "alive recapture with removal".

So, my questions:
1) Is this approach widely used and generally accepted as "good enough"?
2) Are there any studies already that question this approach?
3) Are there any studies which use the ring recoveries from hunting data as alive recaptures, as I suggested?

Thank you very much!

Tomas
